tasks.description: Define a function `greet(name='World')` with a default parameter. Call it once with 'Alice' and once with no argument. Print both results.
tasks.hint:
Default parameter syntax: `def greet(name='World'):`
Calling `greet('Alice')` overrides the default; `greet()` uses 'World'.
Print each call: `print(greet('Alice'))` then `print(greet())`
tasks.solution:
def greet(name='World'):
    return f'Hello, {name}!'

print(greet('Alice'))
print(greet())
tasks.walkthrough:
The first call passes a name, so that name is used.
The second call passes nothing, so `name` takes the default 'World'.

tasks.description: Define a function `total(*numbers)` that accepts any number of arguments and returns their sum. Test with total(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).
tasks.hint:
`*args` collects all extra positional arguments into a TUPLE inside the function.
`def total(*numbers):` — `numbers` is a tuple of everything passed.
`return sum(numbers)` uses Python's built-in sum on the tuple.
tasks.walkthrough:
The star means "collect all the arguments into a tuple called numbers".
`sum()` adds up everything in that tuple, giving 15.

tasks.description: Define a recursive function `factorial(n)` that returns n! (n factorial). Test with factorial(5).
tasks.hint:
Recursion needs a BASE CASE to stop: `if n <= 1: return 1`
Recursive case: `return n * factorial(n - 1)` — calls itself with a smaller n.
`factorial(5)` → `5 * factorial(4)` → ... → `5*4*3*2*1` = 120
tasks.walkthrough:
`factorial(5)` returns `5 * factorial(4)`, which needs `4 * factorial(3)`, and so on down to `factorial(1)`.
That base case returns 1 without calling itself again, so the chain unwinds: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120.

tasks.description: Define a function `describe(**info)` that prints each keyword argument as 'key: value'. Call it with name='Bob', age=30.
tasks.hint:
`**kwargs` collects keyword arguments into a DICT inside the function.
`def describe(**info):` — `info` is `{'name': 'Bob', 'age': 30}`
Loop: `for key, value in info.items(): print(f'{key}: {value}')`
tasks.walkthrough:
Two stars gather the keyword arguments into a dictionary: {'name': 'Bob', 'age': 30}.
Looping over `.items()` prints each key with its value.

tasks.description: Define a function `clamp(value, low, high)` that returns value if it is between low and high, low if below, or high if above. Test: clamp(15, 0, 10) should return 10.
tasks.hint:
The elegant one-liner uses nested min/max: `return max(low, min(value, high))`
`min(value, high)` caps the value at `high`; `max(low, ...)` floors it at `low`.
`clamp(15, 0, 10)` → `max(0, min(15, 10))` → `max(0, 10)` → `10`
tasks.walkthrough:
`min(value, high)` pulls the value down to `high` if it's too big: min(15, 10) is 10.
`max(low, ...)` then pushes it up to `low` if it's too small: max(0, 10) is 10.
The same trick works with an if/elif/else if the nested calls feel cryptic.

tasks.description: Define a function `count_vowels(text)` that returns the number of vowels in a string. Test with 'Hello World'.
tasks.hint:
Loop over each character; check if it's a vowel.
`vowels = 'aeiouAEIOU'` — include both cases.
Count with: `sum(1 for c in text if c in vowels)` or a for loop with a counter.
tasks.walkthrough:
Loop over each character and check whether it appears in the vowels string.
The counter goes up for each match. 'Hello World' has e, o, o, so 3.
A shorter version is `sum(1 for c in text if c in vowels)`.

tasks.description: Define a function `palindrome(word)` that returns True if the word is the same forwards and backwards. Test with 'racecar'.
tasks.hint:
Reverse a string with slicing: `word[::-1]`
Compare the original to the reversed: `return word == word[::-1]`
'racecar' reversed is still 'racecar' → True.
tasks.walkthrough:
`word[::-1]` is the word reversed.
Comparing the original to its reverse gives True only when they're identical.

lesson.intro:
Functions have a few more tricks than you've seen: default values, accepting any
number of arguments, and calling themselves. None of these are things you'll need
every day, but you'll see them in other people's code constantly, so it's worth
knowing what they mean.

sections.heading: Defaults, again
sections.body:
A default makes a parameter optional. Parameters with defaults have to come
after the ones without.
sections.code:
def greet(name='World'):
    return f'Hello, {name}!'

print(greet('Alice'))
print(greet())

sections.heading: *args: any number of arguments
sections.body:
A star before a parameter name collects every extra positional argument into
a tuple. Inside the function you treat it like a list. The name `args` is
only a convention; `numbers` is clearer here.

sections.heading: **kwargs: any number of named arguments
sections.body:
Two stars collect keyword arguments (the `name=value` kind) into a dictionary.
Loop over `.items()` to see them.

sections.heading: Recursion: a function that calls itself
sections.body:
Some problems are naturally defined in terms of a smaller version of
themselves. Factorial of 5 is 5 times factorial of 4. A recursive function
needs two parts: a base case that stops (factorial of 1 is 1) and a recursive
case that calls itself with a smaller input.

Without a base case, the calls never stop and Python gives up with a
RecursionError.

sections.heading: Small useful functions
sections.body:
Two idioms that come up a lot. `max(low, min(value, high))` clamps a value
into a range. `word[::-1]` reverses a string, which makes palindrome checks
a one-liner.

watch_out: Putting a parameter without a default after one with a default is a syntax error.
`*numbers` gives you a tuple. `numbers` alone would be a single argument.
A recursive function with no base case, or one that doesn't shrink the input, never finishes.
`sum()` takes one collection, not separate numbers: `sum([1, 2, 3])` works, `sum(1, 2, 3)` doesn't.
